issues.legal_issue: A litigant who seeks review of an order after pursuing the same relief before a superior court cannot ordinarily maintain the later review application.
material_facts: The respondents challenged the original decision before the High Court and then approached the Supreme Court by special leave petition, which they withdrew.
They pursued review proceedings in the High Court, which were dismissed, and later filed another review application before the Special Court after substantial delay.
The later review sought relief concerning the same original decision.
issues.conclusion: The later review application was an abuse of process and was not maintainable; the High Court should not have entertained a writ petition against its dismissal.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 17-A of the Andhra Pradesh Land Grabbing (Prohibition) Act, 1982, review is available on specified grounds, and Rule 18 of the 1988 Rules prescribes a 30-day limitation. The Court applied the principles in M/s. Kabari Pvt. Ltd. v. Shivnath Shroff, State of Maharashtra v. Prabhakar Bhikaji Ingle, Abbai Maligai Partnership Firm v. K. Santhakumaran, Kunhayammed v. State of Kerala, K. Rajamouli v. A.V.K.N. Swamy, Kumaran Silk Trade (P) Ltd. v. Devendra, and M/s. Green View Tea & Industries v. Collector, Golaghat. A review filed after dismissal of a special leave petition on the same matter ordinarily amounts to abuse of process; a review filed before the special leave petition and still pending when it is dismissed may be considered. The doctrine of merger depends on the jurisdiction exercised, and dismissal of special leave does not itself merge the challenged order into the dismissal order.

predicates.review_application_after_higher_forum_wa: A litigant seeks review of an order after having approached a superior court about that order.
predicates.same_relief_was_pursued_before_that_foru: The litigant sought the same relief from the superior court that the later review application seeks.
predicates.review_was_filed_after_special_leave_was: The litigant filed the review application after the superior court had dismissed the special leave petition.

issues.definition: When a litigant seeks the same relief from a superior court and then files a review after dismissal of the special leave petition, the review application is an abuse of process and is not maintainable.

issues.legal_issue: An agreement to sell, without a completed transfer, does not confer title on the intended purchaser.
material_facts: The vendors had entered into an agreement to sell the land to a cooperative society before executing a registered sale deed in favour of the appellant’s predecessor.
The society had not obtained a decree for specific performance before the registered sale deed was executed.
The respondents produced no evidence that they were members of the society or that the society had allotted the land to them.
issues.conclusion: The agreement to sell did not confer title on the society, while title passed under the registered sale deed in favour of the appellant’s predecessor.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the settled principle that an agreement to sell does not itself create a right or title in favour of the intended buyer. No earlier case or statutory provision is identified in the judgment as the source of this proposition.

predicates.property_title_dispute: The proceeding concerns competing claims to ownership of property.
predicates.only_an_agreement_to_sell_supports_the_c: The claimant relies on an agreement to sell as the basis of the asserted title.
predicates.no_completed_transfer_to_the_claimant: The claimant did not obtain a completed transfer of the property.

issues.definition: In a property title dispute, a claimant relying only on an agreement to sell without a completed transfer does not acquire title through that agreement.

issues.legal_issue: A judgment may be recalled when it was obtained by proven fraud, but an allegation of fraud does not justify reopening matters already adjudicated when the alleged fraud is not established.
material_facts: The respondents alleged that the earlier decision had been obtained by suppression of material information and that the land had not been properly identified.
The issues of alleged fraud, misrepresentation, and land identification had been raised in earlier review and writ proceedings and had been rejected.
The Special Court had examined the land identification through revenue records and found no fraud or misrepresentation.
The respondents did not establish a connection to the land or produce evidence supporting their allegations.
issues.conclusion: The allegations did not justify reopening the earlier adjudication, and the Special Court’s dismissal of the fresh application was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Fraud can vitiate judicial proceedings, and a court has inherent power to recall an order obtained by fraud; when fraud is proved, finality and res judicata do not preserve advantages obtained through it. Suppression of a material document may constitute fraud. But constructive fraud discovered after long delay, or mere proof that a judgment was obtained by perjury, may be insufficient. The Court relied on S.P. Chengalvaraya Naidu v. Jagannath, Lazarus Estate Ltd. v. Besalay, Shrisht Dhawan v. Shaw Brothers, United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Rajendra Singh, Indian Bank v. Satyam Fibres, and Kinch v. Walcott, among other authorities.

predicates.application_seeks_to_reopen_a_final_prop: A litigant applies to reopen a final decision about property by alleging fraud or misrepresentation.
predicates.fraud_is_not_proved: The applicant does not establish that fraud or material suppression occurred.
predicates.alleged_fraud_or_land_identification_was: A court had already considered and decided the allegations of fraud or the identification of the property.

issues.definition: A fraud-based application to reopen a final property decision is not maintainable when fraud is not proved and the same allegations have already been adjudicated.

issues.legal_issue: A person who cannot demonstrate any right or connection to property cannot maintain an application seeking a determination of rights over that property.
material_facts: The respondents produced no document showing that the land had been transferred to the society, that the society had allotted the land to them, or that they were society members.
They produced no other document linking them to the land or establishing a claim to it.
The registered sale deed in favour of the appellant’s predecessor had not been challenged before a competent court.
issues.conclusion: The respondents had no standing to maintain the application, which was not maintainable at their instance.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that an applicant must show a basis for an interest in the property to maintain an application concerning it. It also stated that court proceedings should not be used as a means of harassment or persecution, and that courts should not permit litigants to prolong proceedings without a legitimate basis.

predicates.property_application_seeking_a_determina: The proceeding is an application asking a court to determine rights concerning property.
predicates.applicant_cannot_show_a_connection_to_th: The applicant produces no evidence linking them to the property or establishing a claimed interest in it.

issues.definition: An application to determine rights concerning property is not maintainable at the instance of an applicant who cannot show a connection to that property.

issues.legal_issue: A person in possession cannot be forcibly dispossessed, even if the person is a trespasser, except through due process of law.
material_facts: The appellant’s predecessor received possession of the land under a registered sale deed.
The respondents forcibly occupied the land and raised construction without authorization.
The Special Court ordered their eviction, and the appellant’s predecessor regained possession through execution of that order.
issues.conclusion: The respondents’ forcible dispossession of the appellant’s predecessor was unlawful; possession could be recovered only through the procedure prescribed by law.
issues.legal_principle: Even a trespasser cannot be evicted by force and must be dispossessed through due process. Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, protects a person in possession from dispossession except in due course of law. The Court relied on Midnapur Zamindary Co. Ltd. v. Naresh Narayan Roy, Lallu Yeshwant Singh v. Rao Jagdish Singh, Ram Ratan v. State of U.P., Express Newspapers Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, Krishna Ram Mahale v. Shobha Vankat Rao, and Nagar Palika, Jind v. Jagat Singh, among other authorities.

rule.if: possession_dispute and person_is_in_possession and dispossession_is_attempted_by_force and no_due_process_is_followed

predicates.possession_dispute: The proceeding concerns who is entitled to possess property.
predicates.person_is_in_possession: A person occupies or possesses the property before the attempted dispossession.
predicates.dispossession_is_attempted_by_force: Another person attempts to remove the occupant without that occupant’s consent.
predicates.no_due_process_is_followed: The occupant is not dispossessed through a legally recognized procedure.

issues.definition: A person in possession cannot lawfully be removed by force without a legally recognized procedure, even if that person is a trespasser.
